WON'T DO. Google Play distribution abandoned on 2026-08-22, by the owner's decision, after the Console setup was substantially complete. F-Droid becomes the sole distribution channel.

WHY
Audience fit is the core argument. Pageless is unusable without a self-hosted Pageless server, so most Play installs would be people who bounce off the sign-in screen; F-Droid's audience already IS the self-hosting audience, and the app has been live there since 2026-08-10. The one real Play-only case - a self-hoster's household members who have never heard of F-Droid - did not justify the remaining cost.

That cost was not the setup, which was nearly done, but the gate and the treadmill. The gate: a personal developer account created after 2023-11-13 must run a closed test with 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days, and Play explicitly rejects passive enrolment, so it also demands real engagement and feedback. Worse for this app specifically, testers need a Pageless account as well as a Google account; the chosen approach of one shared demo account would have had 12 people colliding on last-write-wins progress, bookmarks and history, generating false bug reports that would have consumed much of the 14-day window. The treadmill: Play enforces an annual targetSdk bump every 31 August plus recurring policy and Data safety re-attestation, indefinitely. F-Droid imposes none of that.

WHAT IT COST
The 25 USD registration fee, and the package name live.pageless.mobile, which can never be reused on another account. Per Play's inactivity policy, an account created over a year ago that has never submitted an app for review is closed with the fee unrefunded, so the account lapses around 2027-08-05. Reversing this decision before then costs roughly 20 minutes: upload the already-verified AAB to internal testing and verify the account's contact details.

WHAT SURVIVED, AND IT IS NOT LITTLE
  The privacy policy, written, published at https://pageless.live/privacy from a single markdown source, and linked from Settings and the sign-in screen (pm-a6l.7, pm-a6l.6).
  The data flow audit in docs/privacy/data-safety.md, which documents what the app actually transmits - useful independently of any store form.
  API 36 targeting and the Android 16 behaviour-change triage (pm-a6l.4).
  The backup and device-to-device lockdown that keeps the session token on-device (pm-a6l.17), found while preparing the Data safety answers.
  Store metadata under fastlane/metadata/android/en-US, which F-Droid reads, corrected during Play preparation: the description was hard-wrapped so both stores would have rendered hard line breaks mid-sentence, and its bullets would have rendered as literal asterisks.
  Release 861909 from tag 20260822130925-a79739e9d, built and verified, which F-Droid consumes.
  The upload key and its tested restore path, kept in case the decision is revisited.
Several of those were prompted by Play's requirements but are improvements to the app regardless of where it ships.

REPOSITORY CLEANUP with this closure: docs/release/play-signing.md deleted, keystore.properties removed from the repo root, and README and AGENTS references updated. The conditional signing config in app/build.gradle.kts stays, because its unsigned default is what release.yml and F-Droid depend on.

Resolved with option (b): app/src/main/res/xml/network_security_config.xml now lists both <certificates src="system" /> and <certificates src="user" />, cleartext still forbidden. Committed as f368256.

Chosen over (a) keep system-only and over (c) a runtime-toggleable opt-in. (a) would have left private-CA self-hosters unable to use the app at all, and after the Play epic closed those users are a large share of the F-Droid audience. (c) is strictly better on paper - default-deny with a setting, implemented with a delegating X509TrustManager over KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidCAStore") on the shared OkHttp client, which would have covered API, Coil and ExoPlayer in one place - but it puts hand-written trust logic in the path of every request. For a hobby app that is a worse expected outcome than the risk it removes. (d) trust-on-first-use pinning was out of scope: best security story, most code, new UI, easiest to get subtly wrong.

Accepted trade-off, stated plainly in the config comment and in the data-safety finding: a CA installed on the device can intercept app traffic including the bearer token. Installing one is a deliberate trip through Android Settings past explicit warnings and leaves a standing "network may be monitored" notification, so the attacker this enables already controls the device's trust store.

Side effects: the config comment no longer contradicts the config - that contradiction was the original F4 defect. Self-signed certificates now work too, since Android accepts them when installed as a user CA. Finding F4 in docs/privacy/data-safety.md is marked Fixed with the trade-off recorded, and README's "Connecting To A Server" section now tells users the exact Settings path for installing a CA.

Verified in the artifact rather than the source: assembleRelease packages a network security config with both anchors and cleartextTrafficPermitted=false, read back through the manifest's resource id because release builds obfuscate resource filenames. ktlintCheck, lintDebug, testDebugUnitTest and assembleDebug all pass.

Not verified: an actual connection to a server using a private CA. Worth doing opportunistically if a suitable server is available; the change is declarative and low-risk, but nobody has watched it work end to end.
